text.p: Britain's Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc impressed analysts on Friday with a spirited defence of their proposed 24 billion stg merger against counter proposals from rebel shareholder LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton.

"I think there is a bit of positioning in the negotiating process at this stage but they have redressed the balance a bit in their favour after the PR (public relations) machinery of LVMH tipped it their way in the last few weeks," said Nick Lyall, an analyst at SocGen.

Analysts said the two British companies had strengthened their defence by pointing out the onerous tax implications of de-merger proposals from LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault and the fact the merger partners can change their merger arrangements so that only a simple majority of GrandMet shareholders is needed to approve the merger.

"I am certainly more confident they can get it through on their terms although it is always dangerous to under-estimate Arnault. So, if they can, they will still try and include him in the deal," said Nick Williamson, an analyst at Credit Lyonnais.
Under the current proposal 75 percent of GrandMet shareholders need to vote in favour of the merger at an extraordinary meeting to be held in November.

But Guinness finance director Phil Yea told a news conference earlier today this structure was chosen to avoid 70 million stg of stamp duty and could be changed to require only the approval of more than 50 percent of GrandMet shareholders.

Arnault has amassed a stake of about 11 percent in GrandMet in recent weeks, funded by selling Guinness shares, in the belief that GrandMet shares will give him greater influence in his effort to block the merger, said analysts.

This has caused a divergence in Guinness and GrandMet share prices, with the former worth about 10p less at 600p than GrandMet shares. When Guinness and GrandMet announced the deal their share prices were equal.

Arnault is seeking to include LVMH's drinks arm Moet Hennessy in a three-way merger with Guinness' United Distillers and Grand Met's IDV. He wants to name the group DrinksCo, give it a separate listing in Paris and London and take a 35 percent stake in it.
Arnault also wants GMG Brands, the name given to the proposed GrandMet and Guinness merger, to spin off fast food chain Burger King, Guinness brewing and U.S. food producer Pillsbury.
But GrandMet and Guinness said earlier de-merging Pillsbury and Burger King mean a tax hit of 1.5 billion stg.
"I think this is news to Arnault in which case it does do damage to his proposal," said Lyall.

At a news conference earlier today, executives of both Guinness and GrandMet stressed that including LVMH's drinks arm Moet Hennessy would improve GMG Brands but it would have to be at a price which created value for all shareholders.

"I think a compromise should be a reduction in the price that Arnault wants for Moet Hennessy and he should also drop his demand for an immediate de-merger of all three non-spirits businesses," said Ron Littleboy an analyst at Nomura.
"But with at least a commitment to de-merge Guinness brewing, which may not be subject to the same onerous tax implications as Pillsbury and Burger King."

The LVMH demerger proposal for DrinksCo involves the acquisition of LVMH's 66 percent stake in Moet Hennessy for shares in DrinksCo and the folding of LVMH's shareholding in Guinness and Grandmet into further shares in DrinksCo.
Executives told reporters that unlike GMG Brands' other shareholders, LVMH would therefore concentrate its holding into DrinksCo at the expense of other GMG Brands shareholders.
